File picture . <p> The Federal government recently released three major climate documents : the National Climate Risk Assessment ( NCRA ) , the National Adaptation Plan ( NAP ) , including the Agriculture and Land Plan and new emissions reduction targets for 2035 . <h> Try for just $1 for the first month <p> or signup to continue reading <p> Special Offer <p> All articles from our website &amp; app <p> The digital version of This Week 's Paper <p> Our entire network <p> Together , they paint a stark picture of what is ahead under climate change . <p> For agriculture , these reports are more than policy statements . <p> They are a mirror - and what reflects back should prompt us to consider not only our vulnerabilities but also our role in shaping @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ? <p> The public and political reactions to these documents have been immediate , sometimes polarised , and often predictable . <p> Agriculture is frequently drawn into these debates through long-standing political alliances . <p> At times , it can feel as though the concern voiced for our sector is less about agriculture itself and more about maintaining a broader status quo - including support for industries such as fossil fuels . <p> The result is that the positions put forward on our behalf can come across as defensive or dismissive of meaningful climate action , even when that does n't reflect the lived reality of many farmers . <p> This raises a critical question : whose voices are truly shaping our industry 's position on climate ? <p> If we step back from the politics for a moment , we might ask ourselves how our children and grandchildren - who already learn climate science as part of their school curriculum - will look back on the choices we made . <p> Will they see a sector that confronted the challenge head-on , or one that let others speak for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of farmers <p> For many in agriculture , the NCRA is confronting but not surprising . <p> Farmers have lived with the impacts of a changing climate for decades . <p> We remember 2010 - the driest season on record - which set businesses back years . <p> We 've battled extreme bushfires , cyclonic storms , and rare but devastating thunderstorms that tore through power lines and infrastructure . <p> We 've seen the bleaching of Ningaloo Reef , the erosion of our coasts , and the decline of native forests . <p> These are not abstract warnings ; they are lived experiences . <p> Yet , agriculture has adapted with resilience . <p> Across the Wheatbelt and beyond , farm businesses have embraced technology , shifted practices , and become more efficient . <p> Growing season rainfall has declined by 20-30 per cent across large swathes of the Wheatbelt , but we 've kept going . <p> Still , there is a cost . <p> While farms have grown larger and more resilient , our communities have often paid the price . <p> Smaller towns are less recognisable @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ consolidation of farming businesses . <p> Consultants I work with regularly observe that we are tracking toward fewer farms and , in turn , fewer opportunities for community vibrancy . <p> The statistics are sobering : <p> Specialist cropping farms in WA declined by 50pc between 1999-2000 and 2022-23 . <p> Mixed livestock-crop farms in WA declined by 60pc in the same period . <p> The area of chemical fallow has expanded alongside farm size , particularly in the eastern Wheatbelt , as a necessary adaptation to a drier climate . <p> In 2020 , the average broadacre farm in WA spanned 4548 hectares . <p> For some in higher-rainfall zones , climate change has even brought advantages : reduced waterlogging , stronger yields , and thriving systems . <p> For others especially in the northern Wheatbelt - declining rainfall of 20pr or more in already dry regions presents an ongoing challenge . <h> Adaptation is in our DNA - but denial is a dead end <p> No industry adapts better than agriculture . <p> We have to . <p> But adaptation without acknowledging the drivers of change is short-sighted @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ not a concern , or that mitigation will only harm agriculture . <p> This is not just outdated thinking - it risks leaving us behind . <p> Climate change is among the most studied issues in human history . <p> The evidence is overwhelming . <p> Running a farm while waiting for " absolute certainty " would be unthinkable ; why treat climate any differently ? <p> As farmers , we know how to make decisions under uncertainty . <p> We weigh risks , act on evidence , and adapt . <p> The same approach must now guide our industry on climate . <h> The energy transition : from threat to opportunity <p> Even if we set the science aside - and we should not - the national conversation has already moved toward the energy transition . <p> Renewable energy , electrification , and efficiency are often framed as threats . <p> In reality , they represent enormous opportunities if done right : <p> New income streams for farmers hosting renewable infrastructure . <p> Diversified , drought-resilient regional economies . <p> Lower farm input costs and improved efficiency . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ must be respectful and inclusive , but fundamentally , this is not something to fear . <p> It is something to shape and leverage . <p> The same applies to carbon farming . <p> Many farmers already dedicate care and resources to uncleared or less-productive parts of their properties . <p> Registering these areas in carbon projects can turn stewardship into an income stream that supports resilience and succession planning . <p> Carbon markets may not last forever - as global emissions fall , demand for offsets will decline - but that makes it even more important to seize the opportunity now . <h> Farm emissions : A measure of efficiency , not a threat <p> Emissions reduction in agriculture is sometimes viewed as a negative . <p> In reality , emissions are often just lost energy from our systems - a sign that efficiency can be improved . <p> Take nitrogen fertiliser as an example . <p> Every farmer knows the frustration of applying fertiliser and not seeing it fully translate into yield . <p> When nitrogen is n't taken up by the crop , it is lost - @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ losses do n't just hurt profitability ; they also increase nitrous oxide emissions , one of the most potent greenhouse gases . <p> This is where nitrogen use efficiency ( NUE ) becomes so important . <p> Higher NUE means more of the fertiliser we apply ends up in the grain , and less is wasted to the environment . <p> Farmers are already adopting practices that lift NUE - better timing of applications , more precise equipment , and closer matching of fertiliser to crop needs . These changes are n't about ideology ; they are about running a more productive , resilient , and climate-smart business .
